title: In 1519 the Aztec capital was bigger than almost any city in Europe
body: Tenochtitlan stood on an island in Lake Texcoco, joined to the shore by three causeways and supplied with spring water by two aqueducts from Chapultepec. When Hernán Cortés arrived in November 1519, estimates put its population at **200,000 to 400,000 people**; in Europe only Paris, Venice and Constantinople might have rivalled it. Farmers grew crops on chinampas, plots built up in the shallow lake and often misnamed ‘floating gardens’. The city fell in August 1521 after more than two months of fighting, and Mexico City was built on its ruins.

slides.caption: An island city: three causeways, an aqueduct from the west, and a long dike holding back the salty eastern water.

slides.heading: Tenochtitlan next to London, by population
slides.note: At least 200,000 people lived in Tenochtitlan: about five times the London of Henry VIII.

slides.heading: How a city worked on a lake
items: Three causeways, with bridges that could be pulled away
Two terracotta aqueducts over 4 km long from Chapultepec
Chinampas: fields built up in the shallow lakebed
A dike of 12 to 16 km, finished around 1453, kept salty water out

slides.question: By tradition, in what year did the Mexica found Tenochtitlan on its island?
slides.explanation: 1325, by tradition: when Cortés arrived in 1519 the city was less than two centuries old, yet already home to 200,000 people or more.

events.text: Traditional founding date of the Mexica city on the island
The city falls after more than two months of fighting
Its ruins lie in the historic centre of Mexico City

slides.question: What was the 12 to 16 km dike east of the city for?
slides.explanation: Designed by Nezahualcoyotl, ruler of Texcoco, and finished around 1453, the dike kept the fresh spring water around the island separate from the brackish water of the rest of the lake.
